/examples.text: Practical Examples Real marketing systems, real harness decisions This section is reserved for concrete marketing AI case studies: reporting harnesses, content review loops, campaign analysis systems, orchestration flows, and production examples worth dissecting. Status In development now. This module is being prepared as a case-study library for serious marketing AI builders rather than a lightweight examples gallery. Planned examples What this module will cover 01 Reporting Harnesses Implementation walkthroughs of automated reporting systems, data refresh loops, approval checkpoints, and narrative generation pipelines. In development 02 Content and Creative Workflows Breakdowns of briefs, generation, review, routing, and publishing flows that connect models to real editorial and campaign operations. In development 03 Campaign and Analytics Operations Walkthroughs of campaign analysis, anomaly detection, martech orchestration, and the control layers that make those systems operational. In development Editorial direction How the examples library will evolve 01 Each example will focus on one real marketing system shape: what the harness is doing, which deterministic structures hold it together, what tradeoffs the builders made, and where the design breaks under operational pressure.

/learn/system-design/advertising-platfor.text: Harness/System design/Advertising platforms In this guide 01Start with the user experience 02From setting up an ad to reading the report 03What to ask about each platform 04Connect your own software to a platform 05Start with ChatGPT Ads Back to the track System design · Platform overview How advertising platforms work 7 min readUpdated 7 November 2026 An advertising platform brings a campaign into something a person is already doing, such as searching, watching a video or asking for advice. How the platform picks and shows an ad affects what you can learn from the campaign report. On this page 01Start with the user experience 02From setting up an ad to reading the report 03What to ask about each platform 04Connect your own software to a platform 05Start with ChatGPT Ads Use this guide to Follow an ad from campaign setup to the performance report. See which actions show up in the data you can collect. Choose what to explore next, from collecting reports to testing campaign changes. Access No account or API key is needed for this guide. Start with the user experience Begin with what the person is doing: searching for an answer, watching a video, browsing a feed, comparing a product or asking for advice. An ad occupies a particular place in that experience. Where the ad appears shapes what it can look like, what people can do with it and what you can measure. Ask where an ad can appear, which ads qualify and which settings you can change. Then check what the platform counts. An impression records an ad being shown. A conversion is an action you measure, such as a purchase or signup. Each platform has its own rules for counting them. From setting up an ad to reading the report A simplified view of how advertising works 01Set up the campaign 02Choose and show ads 03Measure what people do 04Review results You set the campaign goal, choose the ad content (the creative), set limits on who can see it and decide how much to spend. The platform chooses which ad to show from the ones that qualify. It records actions and groups them into results you can use. Results feed back into later decisions about bids, budgets and ads. How useful they are depends on your goal, how well the numbers capture it, how quickly they arrive and which settings you can change. What to check before using a report When you pull reports into your own tools, check what each number means, whether you have every batch and whether recent figures might change. What to ask about each platform Scroll across to compare all columns → Platform Where people see ads Questions to ask Google Ads Search, YouTube and other places Google shows ads. How do campaign type and placement affect where ads show, how reports group results and which metrics you can compare? Meta Advertising within social experiences, including Facebook and Instagram. How do the ad, campaign goal and measured actions relate to the results in the report? Amazon Ads Advertising around shopping and media experiences. What can you learn from campaign reports, and when do you need to combine data or build audiences? TikTok Ads as people discover and watch videos. Which views, interactions and later actions can your software collect? ChatGPT Ads Advertising in the context of exploration and decisions in a conversation. How are ads chosen, what can advertisers change and what can they measure? Programmatic: DV360 & The Trade Desk Buying and measuring ads across many publishers’ sites and apps. Which tools let you set up campaigns, create reports and download every batch of results? Use these questions to compare platforms. Check each platform’s rules for choosing ads, organising campaigns and deciding which ads get credit for a conversion. Amazon Marketing Cloud helps advertisers analyse data and build audiences alongside their campaign reports. It’s a clean room, a controlled space for working with data under privacy rules. Amazon Marketing Cloud overview Connect your own software to a platform Setting up ads, sending records of actions and collecting performance results are separate jobs. They may use different APIs, which are the ways your software asks the platform for data or actions. For example, Google directs DV360 performance reporting to the Bid Manager API. Campaign management uses the Display & Video 360 API. DV360 reporting boundary Choose the account and dates. Decide how to group results, such as by campaign and day, and check each metric’s units and meaning. Keep track of which batches you’ve collected, which reports are still running and why any data is missing. Save the original results, avoid counting a record twice and make it possible to pick up after an interruption. Flag late or revised data. A successful request can return figures that will still change. When you use a report to make a decision, explain what it covers and what is still uncertain. Pagination fetches the next batch of the same report. Splitting a request asks for several smaller reports. Streaming lets you read a large file as it arrives. Whichever approach you use, check that you have every batch you asked for. Start with ChatGPT Ads The ChatGPT Ads guide follows an ad from the conversation where it might appear to the report an advertiser can read. The reporting example shows how your software can ask for daily campaign results and flag gaps. Start with the platform guide to see how the parts fit together. If you’re already working on a reporting tool, start with the API design principles. /learn/system-design/api-design.text: Harness/System design/API design In this guide 01Start with the task 02Define the contract 03Keep the meaning when data moves 04Make failures useful 05Apply the principles in a case Back to the track System design · Reusable principles API design principles 8 min readUpdated 8 November 2026 An API (application programming interface) gives software a way to ask another system for data or to take an action. A good API tells you what you can ask for, what will change and what the result actually shows. Read these guides in any order API principlesDesign a clear request How ads workSee how ads are chosen Advertiser APIsFind the tool you need Reporting exampleCollect campaign results On this page 01Start with the task 02Define the contract 03Keep the meaning when data moves 04Make failures useful 05Apply the principles in a case Use this guide to Describe the task before choosing how to run it. Explain what the task covers, what it changes and when it is done. Use the same rules when a person, an app or an AI agent runs the task. Before you start The examples use HTTP, the rules software follows to send a request over the web and receive a reply. No account or API key is needed for this guide. Start with the task Write down who is making the request, what it covers and what they should get back. “Get last week’s campaign results” and “change the campaign budget” can use the same API. One reads data and the other changes a setting. What happens when you ask an API to do something 01Define the task 02Check permissions and details 03Run the task within its limits 04Explain the result Put permission checks and limits in the code that runs the task. Those rules should apply whether someone uses a web request, a command-line interface (CLI) for typed commands, or an AI agent connected through the Model Context Protocol (MCP). Define the contract A contract is the set of rules a request and its result must follow. For a report, it covers details such as who can ask for it, which dates it includes and how to tell whether data is missing. Part of the contract What to decide Identity and permission Who can make the request, which accounts or records they can use, and where the system checks permission. Inputs What you must supply, what the system assumes if you leave something blank, and which units and dates it accepts. Effects Whether the task reads data or changes it, and how to check what happened. Results How to tell a finished task from an empty result, a partial result, a refused request or a service that could not respond. Limits How much work the system will do, how long it will wait and how to continue or stop. Source of the data Where the data came from, when it was recorded, what was changed and what is still uncertain. A server can successfully receive a request while the report is still being prepared. A valid account ID can belong to someone else. Make the result say whether the task is finished and whether the requester has permission. Keep the meaning when data moves If you reformat a report or calculate a new metric, keep the original IDs and units alongside the result. Mark an unavailable number as missing so readers can distinguish it from a measured zero. For a list or report, explain how results are ordered and how to tell when you have the last batch. For a change such as a budget update, explain how to recognise a repeat request. If the first attempt times out, check whether it took effect before trying again. Give your report format a version so readers and software know how to interpret it. If you change what a field means, use a new version and explain the change. For example, a report grouped by the date of an ad interaction answers a different question from one grouped by the date of a purchase. Make failures useful Condition What the result should tell you Empty The system checked the requested account, dates or records and found no matches. Partial Which results are available, which are missing and how to continue or why the task stopped. Rejected What was wrong with the request or which permission is needed. Keep passwords, keys and private data out of the message. Unavailable Whether you can safely try again, how many attempts to make and where to pick up. Unconfirmed change A request ID and a way to check whether the change happened before you repeat it. Give people a short explanation. Give apps and agents a consistent code for each reason and a clear next step. Apply the principles in a case The ChatGPT Ads reporting case shows how these rules work in practice. You choose the account and dates, collect every batch of results and make any gaps visible in the report. Find the API you need Use the advertiser API guide to find the right tool. Open the reporting example for a sample request. The platform guide explains how ads are chosen, shown and measured. Next · Worked example · Preview How to collect ChatGPT Ads reports Apply the contract to a daily campaign report and see how the response explains missing data. Read the reporting case Where to go next Related guides Advertiser API guide ChatGPT Ads APIs for advertisers See which ChatGPT Ads tools let you set up ads, send conversion data and read performance reports. The wider context Related reading The Muscles of the Machine How software and AI agents use tools, and why each tool needs a clear job, rules and limits.

/learn/system-design/chatgpt-ads-apis.text: Harness/System design/Advertiser APIs In this guide 01What advertisers can do 02How to read the internal tools in our examples 03API documentation and downloads Back to the track System design · Advertiser API guide ChatGPT Ads APIs for advertisers 6 min readUpdated 8 November 2026 Use this map to find the tool for your task. An API is how your software asks a platform for data or sends it instructions. ChatGPT Ads has separate tools for changing ad settings, sending records of actions like purchases and reading campaign results. Read these guides in any order API principlesDesign a clear request How ads workSee how ads are chosen Advertiser APIsFind the tool you need Reporting exampleCollect campaign results On this page 01What advertisers can do 02How to read the internal tools in our examples 03API documentation and downloads Use this guide to Find the right API for the job you want to do. Check what data you can send or receive. See what access each tool requires. Access No account or API key is needed for this guide. What advertisers can do OpenAI advertiser APIs · Guide by Harness · Reviewed 2026-11-08 The arrows show where data goes. This map is based on OpenAI’s documentation. Live account checks are planned. 01 · Advertiser task Set up campaigns and ads Your software → Campaign settings Change the settings the ad system uses to choose and show ads. API to use Create, read, update or delete campaigns, ad groups and ads through api.ads.openai.com/v1 Data available IDs, status, budgets and bids. Context hints (context_hints) describe situations where an ad may be relevant. Creative fields include the title, ad text and destination link (creative.title, creative.body and creative.target_url). What to watch for You can change advertiser settings. Conversation details, ranking scores and individual auction results stay inside the platform. Access Keep the Advertiser API key on your server. The key gives your software access to a specific ad account. Some features require separate access. Campaign setup and management · More API details 02 · Advertiser task Send records of conversions Your server → OpenAI’s measurement system Send a record when someone takes an action you track, such as placing an order. API to use POST https://bzr.openai.com/v1/events?pid=<PIXEL-ID> Data available Send an event ID, the type of action, the time in milliseconds (timestamp_ms), permitted details for matching and other information about the action. The API responds with information about the submission. What to watch for Accepting a record, giving an ad credit for the action and finding out whether the ad caused an extra sale are three separate things. To avoid counting an action twice when you send it from both your website and server, use the same event ID and Pixel ID. Access You need a Pixel ID, which identifies the measurement setup, and a Conversions API key. Get them through Ads Manager or an approved partner setup. Conversions API 03 · Advertiser task Get performance reports OpenAI’s reporting API → Your software Request totals such as impressions, clicks and spend for the account, campaigns or ads you choose. API to use GET /ad_account/insights GET /campaigns/{campaign_id}/insights GET /ad_groups/{ad_group_id}/insights GET /ads/{ad_id}/insights POST /conversions/insights Data available Results grouped by account, campaign, ad group or ad and by time period. Conversion reports have their own definitions and limits. What to watch for General Insights can send a report in batches. A conversion report that is too large needs smaller requests. The reporting example shows how to handle each. Access Keep the Advertiser API key on your server and check your account has the reporting features you need. Add the paths above to https://api.ads.openai.com/v1. Insights reference · More API details How to read the internal tools in our examples OpenAI describes how its system finds, checks and ranks ads before an auction. The exact messages those parts exchange are private. Names like prepare_queries, embed and final_gate belong to our example of how a system like this might work. OpenAI engineering account What the reporting case can answer How often were your ads shown and how much did you spend in the campaigns and dates you chose? Conversation details, relevance scores and the reasons for individual auction results stay inside the platform. API documentation and downloads Use OpenAI’s documentation for the exact requests your software can send. The Harness downloads use made-up examples to explain how you might model ad selection or collect reports. Explore the case by track System designDefine the report contract Algorithms & dataCheck that you have every batch Software & productionHandle an interrupted report Measurement & MLInterpret credited conversions AI engineeringGive an agent a bounded reporting tool Run the samples locally Decide what the report should cover Start with results by campaign and day for one ad account you have permission to use. Choose the dates and metrics, then keep the account’s time zone, currency and the time you collected the data with the report. A live request needs separate Advertiser API access. Reporting definitions and data updates Harness example of how to collect and save a report 01Request data from your server 02Collect results in batches 03Save data and progress 04Show results and gaps Reports show totals for the campaigns or ads you ask about. Individual conversations, the ads considered for them and their ranking scores stay inside the platform. Keep the Ads API key, a secret your software uses to sign in, on your server. Authentication and account scope Define the result before choosing the interface. Return the requested scope, the scope actually covered, and a status with the reason collection stopped. A subtotal should identify the rows it covers so the caller can tell whether it answers the original question. Explore System design Ask Insights for daily campaign results Insights is the part of the Ads API that returns performance reports. This request asks for one row per campaign per day, with the campaign ID, date, impressions, clicks and spend. Insights request reference Example API request · sample dateshttp GET https://api.ads.openai.com/v1/ad_account/insights aggregation_level=campaign time_granularity=daily fields[]=metadata.readable_time fields[]=campaign.id fields[]=campaign.impressions fields[]=campaign.clicks fields[]=campaign.spend time_ranges[]={"type":"unix_range","start":1793491200,"end":1793577600} # Query values must be URL-encoded. # Authorisation is supplied by your server, never this page. This request covers 1 November 2026 in UTC, the time standard used for the example. The end time is midnight at the start of 2 November, so the request excludes that day. Check the account’s reporting time zone if you want a local calendar day. The download labels OpenAI’s request fields and our own report fields separately. Check that you have every batch Interface How to get the full result General Insights Insights sends results in batches called pages. Save first_id, last_id and has_more. If has_more is true, send the same request with after set to the last_id from that page. Stop when has_more is false. Dedicated conversion report A request to POST /conversions/insights can return error 413 if the report is too large. In that case you get no rows or marker for a next page. Split the request by campaign or other ID, or use shorter date ranges that do not overlap. Local sample collector Track the page markers already seen and the campaign and date pairs already accepted. Stop on a repeated marker or duplicate row and retain the earlier valid batches. Pagination means asking for the next page of the same result. Splitting an oversized conversion report means making several smaller requests and combining their results. Use the rules for the report you asked for. Reporting limits Explore Algorithms & data Show what your report is missing Sample report from Harness · made-up datajson { "reference_kind": "illustrative-reporting-envelope", "account_ref": "sample-account", "status": "partial", "coverage": {"completed_partitions": 2, "expected_partitions": 3}, "missing_partitions": ["campaign-group-c"], "stop_reason": "retry_budget_exhausted" } In this example, two of three batches are ready and the remaining batch is named. Give temporary failures a bounded retry budget. If access is denied or the results cannot be validated, stop and return the batches you already accepted with the reason the report is incomplete. To resume across runs in production, save the original request, accepted batches, and the next cursor. Use the campaign and date to avoid counting a row twice within this report. When figures arrive late, reconcile the newer snapshot for the same scope instead of adding both snapshots together. Try a retry or a partial run The local collector can retry a simulated temporary failure and return accepted rows when it stops early. Each invocation starts a fresh run. Durable checkpoints and live deployment are in development. Explore Software & production Can you use this report? Prepared examples · Fictional data The request in each example Get daily impressions, clicks, spend and credited conversions for campaigns in a fictional UK ad account on 1 and 2 November 2026. Time zone and currency London time, GBP Conversion credit 30 days after a click or one day after a view. Results use the date of the ad interaction. Open an example to see what came back and what you can do with it. Complete reportThe final batch arrived What came back Both batches arrived, giving you three rows. Each row covers one campaign and day. Impressions 2,300 Clicks 64 Spend £36.00 Credited conversions Total unavailable One row shows zero conversions and another has no conversion count. The spend total covers all the returned rows, but there isn’t enough information to add up conversions. What to do next Use the spend total for the requested period. Record when you collected it and check for later updates before using recent figures to make a decision. Empty reportThe request finished with zero rows What came back The first batch was empty and said there were no more batches. There are no totals to show. No rows matched the request. That gives you no spend or conversion figures to interpret. What to do next Check the account, dates and filters. If those are right, report “no rows returned” and keep the totals blank. Partial reportAnother batch is missing What came back The first batch returned two rows and a marker for the next batch. The next batch never arrived. Rows received 2 Spend in rows received £30.50 £30.50 is the subtotal for the rows you have. The spend for the full period is still unknown. What to do next Keep the original dates and filters and use the saved marker to retry the missing batch. If you can’t recover it, label the report partial and carry the gap into any summary. Stale reportAll batches arrived, but the figures are old What came back At a review on 5 November, the team still had a complete report collected on 3 November. They refreshed the same dates and received revised figures. Same reporting dates, two collection times Metric 3 Nov, 09:00 5 Nov, 09:00 Spend £36.00 £36.30 Credited conversions Unavailable 3 Receiving every batch tells you the collection finished. It doesn’t tell you whether the platform has since updated the figures. What to do next Refresh the same request before using the old copy. Use the newer figures for the same dates, and retain both collection times so readers can see what changed. Rejected requestThe requester lacked access What came back In this example, the reporting tool refused the request because the signed-in person didn’t have permission for the selected account. It returned no report. The tool stopped at its access check. There are no figures to interpret for that account. What to do next Check that you selected the right account and ask an account admin to confirm your access. Retry once the account or permission has been corrected. Interpret credited conversions Before comparing reports, check that the account, dates, time zone, currency, and attribution settings match. Check coverage and freshness too. An unavailable conversion count represents missing information. A newer snapshot may have a different count for the same dates. An attributed conversion is an action the platform credits to an ad under its reporting rules. To estimate how many additional sales the campaign caused, define the outcome and compare it with a credible estimate of what would have happened without the campaign. A suitable holdout can provide that comparison. Explore Measurement & ML Give an agent a bounded reporting tool Give the tool one job: read a campaign report within an explicit scope. For a live design, the service should enforce account access and request limits. Return the scope, status, coverage, and freshness alongside the values so an agent can explain an incomplete result before recommending a decision. The local MCP tool reads the bundled fictional reports. Its inputs select a scenario and a page limit. Try the partial scenario and check whether the agent can explain which totals are available and why collection stopped. The collector and adapter run instructions are below. The ad experience OpenAI describes ChatGPT advertising around moments when people explore options, compare alternatives and make decisions in a conversation. That makes the surrounding task and context part of the starting point for understanding an ad’s relevance. ChatGPT advertiser overview For an advertiser, the next questions are practical. Which settings can you change? Which actions can you measure? Which results can your software pull into a report? Dashed boxes show how Harness proposes to collect and save reports. Sources reviewed 8 November 2026. ChatGPT Ads · how the parts fit togetherSolid: OpenAI documentedDashed: Harness proposal Scroll sideways to see the rest of the diagram → OpenAI · documentedOne exchange in chat OpenAI · documentedWrite the answer OpenAI · documentedChat screen OpenAI · documentedAd session tracks the chat OpenAI · documentedAd orchestrator OpenAI · documentedFind possible ads OpenAI · documentedCheck which ads qualify OpenAI · documentedScore possible ads OpenAI · documentedAd auction OpenAI · documentedAd blocked by check OpenAI · documentedFinal check for fit OpenAI · documentedAd and introduction OpenAI · documentedArrives too late to show OpenAI · documentedCheck arrival time OpenAI · documentedEvents and feedback OpenAI · documentedReporting API Harness · proposedSaved report data Harness · proposedReport collector Arrows that point both ways show a request and its reply, or a tool the system can use again. The final check can stop an ad before it is sent. An ad that arrives late has already been sent and misses its chance to appear. Example ad outcomes Eligible and on time. The ad can reach the chat screen in time. Count an impression once you know the ad was shown. Ad arrives too late. The ad system sends the ad, but it arrives too late for the chat to show it. No ad is shown in this exchange, so there is no impression to count. ChatGPT still answers. Final context check fails. The final check rejects the ad for this conversation before the system sends it to the chat screen. No ad appears, so there is no impression to count. These examples use imagined situations to show how an ad can be chosen and still go unseen. OpenAI documented · Simplified 1. How the answer and ad take separate paths ChatGPT writes the answer separately from choosing an ad. The answer does not wait for an ad. What this means in practice If you add advertising to a product, keep the main feature usable even when the ad system is slow or unavailable. What to check Follow the top row from the conversation to the answer on screen. OpenAI engineering account OpenAI documented · Simplified 2. Find ads that could fit the conversation The ad session keeps track of the conversation. An AI model called the orchestrator decides when to use tools that find, check and score possible ads. It can use a tool more than once. What this means in practice An ad can match what someone is looking for and still fail a check, for example if its campaign has run out of budget. What to check Follow the arrows between the orchestrator and the tools it can use. OpenAI engineering account See six steps involved in choosing an ad OpenAI documented · Simplified 3. See when a selected ad appears The auction chooses an ad and sets its price. A final check can stop it if it does not fit the conversation. An ad that passes the check can still arrive too late for the chat to show it. What this means in practice Keep separate records for when an ad is chosen, sent and shown. An impression counts an ad that was shown. What to check Try the example outcomes. Watch what happens to the ad while the answer carries on. OpenAI engineering account OpenAI documented · Simplified 4. Find the results advertisers can read OpenAI describes recording events and collecting feedback. Its reporting API gives advertisers performance totals. What this means in practice Before using a report to make a decision, check which ads and dates it covers, what each number measures and when it was collected. What to check The diagram shows the event records and reporting API separately. The public description covers them as separate topics. OpenAI reporting documentation See what advertisers can do with the APIs · How OpenAI records events and feedback Harness proposal · Planned 5. See how you could collect reports The dashed boxes show our plan for software that collects reports and saves the results, including which dates they cover and when they were collected. What this means in practice Decide how to split large requests, where to save the results and when to try again if a request fails. What to check Use the reporting case to see how your software can show which results are ready and which are missing. OpenAI reporting documentation Open the reporting example What this diagram is based on OpenAI describes what each part does. The diagram groups those parts to make the process easier to follow. The report collector and saved report data are part of a planned Harness build. How ChatGPT looks for a relevant ad The orchestrator is the AI model that decides which ad selection tools to use. Open each step to see what it starts with and what it produces. The model can go back to a tool when it needs to. Source: OpenAI’s engineering account The steps below describe work that happens inside OpenAI. Advertiser reports give you campaign results. See what advertisers can do with the APIs. 01Work out what someone is looking for Based on OpenAI’s description Details from the conversationSearches for products or services The orchestrator turns relevant details from the chat into searches for ads. It can revise those searches as the person’s goal becomes clearer. Harness example If someone asks for lightweight shoes for a rainy city break, the system might look for “water-resistant walking shoes” or “packable travel footwear”. What this means for advertisers Describe what your product actually helps people do. Test whether that message performs well. The system can look for related meanings as well as matching words. 02Find ads with a similar meaning Based on OpenAI’s description Searches based on the chatPossible ads The system turns the meaning of each search into a list of numbers called an embedding. It compares these numbers with those for ads in several searchable collections to find close matches quickly. Harness example In our example, one tool creates the numbers and another looks for matches. The numbers and search settings in the download are made up. What this means for advertisers Keep product details accurate and make sure the landing page matches the ad. The search that led to an individual ad stays inside the platform. 03Check which ads qualify Based on OpenAI’s description Possible adsAds that pass the checks The system can check whether the ad is active, fits the audience and placement, follows policy and has budget left. It can also spread spending over time (pacing) and remove repeated candidates. Harness example A walking shoe ad might fit a conversation about a trip, but the campaign might only run in France while the person is in Canada. What this means for advertisers If an ad rarely shows, check where it can run and whether the campaign has budget before rewriting the copy. 04Score relevance and quality Based on OpenAI’s description Ads that qualifyAds with scores The system can score how well an ad fits the person’s goal, how likely people are to interact with it and how it performed before. Harness example Our example uses made-up scores between 0 and 1 so you can see what a scoring result might look like. OpenAI keeps its scoring rules and scores private. What this means for advertisers Compare versions of an ad with a test that you can explain. Click-through rate divides clicks by impressions and shows the result as a percentage. The platform’s own scores stay private. 05Shortlist ads and run the auction Based on OpenAI’s description Ads that fit the chatAd choice and price The orchestrator shortlists ads. The auction decides which can compete, uses quality as part of the ranking, then picks the ad and sets the price. Harness example The download includes a made-up bid and price to show what an auction record could contain. Use OpenAI’s documentation for billing rules. What this means for advertisers Track what you bid and what you were charged separately. Use campaign results to assess performance. The reasons for an individual auction result stay private. 06Check the fit and show the ad on time Based on OpenAI’s description Selected ad and current conversationAd blocked, sent or shown The final check can stop an ad that feels out of place in the conversation. An ad can also pass the check and be sent, yet arrive too late to show. Harness example In our example, one record says whether the ad passed the final check. Another says whether it arrived late or was shown. What this means for advertisers Use impressions to count ads that were shown. Keep a timing problem separate from a decision to block an ad. The conversation and the details of how individual ads were chosen stay inside the platform. Ad system examples to download Use OpenAI’s documentation for the exact requests your software can send. What advertisers can set up and measure The advertising workflow from setup to reporting 01Configure campaigns & ads 02Show ads 03Record actions 04Review results An ad account contains campaigns, campaigns contain ad groups, and ad groups contain ads. An API is how software sends a request to another system. The Advertiser API lets software manage campaigns and request reports. When you build a report, keep each campaign’s ID and settings alongside its results. Advertiser API and campaign structure A measurement pixel is a small piece of website code that records actions. The Conversions API lets your server send records of actions such as purchases. Sending those records and requesting a campaign report are separate jobs. Measurement interfaces An Ads API key is a secret your server uses to access a specific ad account. Using ChatGPT and getting advertiser API access are separate. Before connecting a live account, check that you have access and that the features you need are available. The reasons an ad was considered, scored or chosen for a particular conversation stay inside the platform. Get campaign results The advertiser API guide shows which tools to use. With conversion-optimised cost per click (CPC), the campaign aims for a chosen action, such as a purchase, and you pay for valid clicks. It requires an eligible ad account and conversion tracking. An order credited to an ad tells you how the platform counted it. To estimate how many extra sales the ad caused, you need a comparison. Conversion-optimised campaign requirements Before changing a budget or ad, check what the report measures and whether more data may arrive. The measurement guides will look at how to use these results and how to estimate the extra sales a campaign caused, known as incrementality. /learn/measurement-ml/attribution-and-li.text: Harness/Measurement & ML/Attribution and lift In this guide 01Choose the outcome before you look at results 02Compare results with and without the campaign 03Work through a fictional example Back to the track Measurement & ML · Reusable guide How to compare attributed conversions and lift 4 min readUpdated 10 November 2026 Say you need to decide whether to raise next month’s ad budget. An ad report can tell you which orders it credits to the campaign. An experiment can help you estimate how many extra orders the campaign caused. On this page 01Choose the outcome before you look at results 02Compare results with and without the campaign 03Work through a fictional example Use this guide to Choose an outcome that would change your decision. Read attributed conversions and estimated lift as answers to different questions. Write down what evidence would justify acting on a result. Access No account or API key is needed for this guide. Choose the outcome before you look at results Write down the decision, the outcome, and the period. For example, decide whether to raise the budget based on completed orders over two weeks. Count orders from every channel using the same rules for everyone in the comparison. Attribution is the rule an ad platform uses to credit an outcome. For example, a report may count an order when someone buys within a set number of days after clicking an ad. Some of those customers might have ordered anyway. Compare results with and without the campaign When you can, randomly assign eligible people to two groups. Make the campaign available to one group and withhold it from the other. The second group is called a holdout. Compare everyone assigned to each group, including people who never clicked or saw an ad. If you can run the campaign separately by region, another option is to randomly assign regions to the two groups. You need enough suitable regions and a way to limit spillover, such as people in the holdout seeing the test ads. Google Research on geographic experiments Work through a fictional example Imagine you assign 10,000 eligible people to each group and track orders for two weeks. Each person can place at most one order in this example. The platform credits the campaign with 180 orders under its reporting rules. Scroll across to compare all columns → Group People assigned Completed orders Order rate Campaign available 10,000 260 2.6% Holdout 10,000 200 2.0% The campaign group had 60 more orders. Because the groups are the same size, subtracting the counts gives the same comparison as subtracting the rates. The difference is 0.6 percentage points, or 30% above the holdout rate. This difference estimates incremental lift, the extra effect caused by the campaign. The 180 credited orders came from a separate reporting rule. Write a decision rule before the test Decide how many extra orders you would need to cover the cost of the ads. Check the range of effects that fit the data, since another sample could give a different result. If that range includes results too small to cover the cost, collect more evidence or hold the budget steady. Read security architecture From the source analysis Where each structure sits in the agent stack 01 Skills BFS, DFS, topological sort, Bloom filters, and circular buffers keep workflow steps explicit and bounded. 02 Tools and MCP Binary search, heaps, Rabin-Karp, and routing algorithms make structured tool responses fast, auditable, and safe to inspect. 03 Plugins and Memory Plugin packages rely on memory windows, indexes, dependency graphs, and portable execution rules. 04 Orchestration Topological sort, Dijkstra, Union-Find, and lease-locked queues turn multi-agent work into schedulable, recoverable paths. 05 Control Plane Approval state machines, token buckets, permission graphs, and audit hash chains enforce identity, policy, rate limits, and tamper-evident logs. Ad platform control plane Plan, validate, approve, execute, record 01 Plan Agent drafts a change The read-only agent proposes a structured DV360 or Google Ads diff: entity, current state, proposed state, rationale, expected impact, and risk tier. change_plan.json → 02 Validate Policy checks scope and risk The policy engine checks advertiser scope, max bid or budget delta, targeting breadth, workspace ownership, and same-entity write conflicts. policy_decision → 03 Approve Human signs high-risk action Budget increases, targeting broadening, audience expansion, and tracking changes create an approval record before execution can continue. approval_id → 04 Execute Narrow service writes to API The executor retrieves scoped credentials, validates current platform state, applies the approved change, and queues same-line-item DV360 writes. execution_grant → 05 Record Audit captures rollback evidence The system stores pre-image, post-image, API payload, policy result, approver, execution token, and rollback patch for review or recovery. audit_event Scoped campaign-change grant One action, one advertiser, one expiry window The campaign equivalent of a scoped payment token: enough authority to apply one approved change, not broad access to the whole ad account. { "platform": "dv360", "advertiser_id": "987654", "entity_type": "line_item", "allowed_action": "apply_bid_delta", "max_delta_percent": 10, "approval_id": "approval_abc" } Implementation notes How this mirrors the reference pattern 01 The published analysis provides the systems argument and the six operation model: find, explore, order, deduplicate, route, and compress. /learn/ai-engineering/control-plane.text: Harness/AI Engineering/Control plane Structural Patterns Agent Control Plane Identity, gateway, policy, inspection, and audit are the structures that let marketing agents touch real systems without becoming unmanaged automations. This reference pattern turns the security architecture into a practical harness pattern. Source Related reading from AI Knowledge Hub: Secure Marketing Agents. The article develops an execution architecture; this pattern explores the control plane that marketing teams need before agents touch campaign data, commerce feeds, or publishing workflows. Read article Try the offline mock lab Reference pattern A governed route from agent intent to system action AgentCampaign optimization agent Plans the work, but does not hold platform credentials. ↓ GatewayIdentity + policy boundary Checks scope, account access, protocol rules, and approval gates. ↓ ToolsGoogle Ads · DV360 · BigQuery · CMS Run with scoped credentials owned by the gateway, not the agent. ↓ AuditAction trail Records actor, account, tool, decision, approver, and result. Wrong default Personal OAuth as agent identity The agent inherits a human account, sees whatever the person sees, and breaks when the person leaves, rotates credentials, or changes roles. Audit also becomes ambiguous because human and agent actions collapse into one identity. Safer pattern Agent identity behind a gateway The agent authenticates to the gateway. The gateway owns platform credentials, applies account-level policy, runs inspection, and logs the action trail separately from human activity. Control layers What the harness must provide 01 Agent Identity Give every agent its own identity, scope, owner, and lifecycle instead of letting it borrow a human OAuth session. 02 Gateway Route every tool call through one controlled boundary that can enforce account access, protocol rules, and approval gates. 03 Policy Define which accounts, tools, budgets, write actions, and data classes the agent can touch before execution begins. 04 Inspection Scan prompts, tool arguments, URLs, and responses for injection, leakage, unsafe destinations, and policy violations. 05 Audit Log agent actions separately from human actions, including scope, tool, input hash, output hash, status, and approver. Execution path How a campaign data request should move 01 Agent requests campaign metrics 02 Gateway checks agent identity 03 Policy resolves allowed accounts 04 Tool call runs with scoped credentials 05 Audit log stores the action trail Approval gates Risk decides whether the agent can act ActionRiskControl Read campaign metricsLowAllow if account scope matches the agent policy. Export customer-level dataHighBlock by default or require security approval and redaction. Change campaign budgetHighRequire human approval, budget cap, and post-action audit event. Publish creativeMediumRequire brand and compliance review before the tool call executes. Skills · Run locally Review evidence before approving an action Before a reviewer approves a campaign action, they need to know which data the agent used and how it checked the result. The ChatGPT Advertising Experiment Plugin 0.2.0 lets you inspect that evidence with fictional account and campaign data. View the Skills release manifest for 0.2.0 Use Python 3.9 or newer and run these commands from the Skills repository. If you need to build ./bin/skills-hub, install Go and run make cli-build there first. Open the Skills repository Installation downloads the pinned release into a temporary directory. The mock run then uses the bundled data without credentials or network access. Open the plugin in the Skills catalogue Install and run the local mock lab lab_dir=$(mktemp -d) && ./bin/skills-hub install \ --source remote --module plugins \ --registry-url https://skills.ai-knowledge-hub.org/registry/plugins-index.json \ --entry marketing/chatgpt-advertising-experiment-plugin@0.2.0 \ --runtime codex --execution-runtime python3 \ --target "$lab_dir/plugins" --cache-dir "$lab_dir/cache" && cd "$lab_dir/plugins/marketing/chatgpt-advertising-experiment-plugin" && python3 scripts/run_mock_lab.py Open output/mock-evidence-bundle.json in the installed plugin directory. The sample records zero network calls and one valid test conversion. In a separate matching example, it finds two event records, removes one duplicate, and matches one business outcome. Check those counts before using the bundle to inform a review. The lab exercises the evidence step. A live account read requires separate setup and verification, and the release has no live write adapter. To practise collecting report pages and handling missing results, try the separate Harness sample collector. Monday morning checklist Questions to ask before deploying an agent 01 Does the agent have its own identity, or does it inherit a person's credentials? 02 Can access be revoked without touching the human account? 03 Which gateway sees every outbound tool call? 04 Which actions require approval before execution? 05 Can the audit log separate agent activity from human activity?

/learn/ai-engineering/verify-small-code-.text: Harness/AI engineering/Verify a small code change In this guide 01Give the agent one change and a clear boundary 02Check the broken input and a working input 03Give the reviewer evidence they can use 04Run the versioned Skills example locally Back to the track AI Engineering & Harnesses · Reusable guide Verify a small code change with an agent 5 min readUpdated 10 November 2026 Imagine an internal package installer accepts an empty package identifier. You ask a coding agent to fix it. Before you accept the change, you need evidence that the installer now rejects empty input and still accepts a valid package. On this page 01Give the agent one change and a clear boundary 02Check the broken input and a working input 03Give the reviewer evidence they can use 04Run the versioned Skills example locally Use this guide to Describe the repair and the behaviour it must preserve. Compare what happens before and after the change using a check you trust. Record what passed and what remains unverified. Access No account or API key is needed for this guide. Give the agent one change and a clear boundary Describe the problem in terms you can check. Here, an identifier is the name the installer uses to look up a package. The installer should reject an empty name before it tries to find or install anything. An example request Reject an empty package identifier before lookup. Keep the existing behaviour for valid identifiers. Reproduce the failure, make the smallest change, and show the files changed, the checks you ran, and anything you could not verify. Leave the decision to merge with the reviewer. Check the broken input and a working input Run the checks on the original version to establish what happens today. In this example, empty input reaches the package lookup. Use a fake lookup that records whether it was called, so you can check where validation happens without touching a real package service. Repeat the same checks on the proposed change. Input What the check should show after the change Empty identifier The installer reports an invalid identifier and makes no lookup call. Valid identifier The installer looks up the requested package and returns the expected result. Read the diff, the list of what changed. Check that the agent left the valid path intact. Rerun the checks yourself or use a trusted automated runner. If the agent changed the tests, inspect the new expectations and confirm the empty-input check fails on the original code for the expected reason. A green run is useful only if it still checks the behaviour you care about. Give the reviewer evidence they can use Record the version checked, the command and its observed result, and the limits of the run. For example, a local check with a fake lookup can prove that the installer skips lookup for empty input. It leaves compatibility with a live package service unverified. If a required check could not run, record what blocked it and keep the review open. These checks help you decide whether to accept this one change. To evaluate the agent itself, repeat the exercise across different tasks and failure conditions. The Code Agent’s Playbook in Related reading shows how to design that wider evaluation. Run the versioned Skills example locally The Code Maintenance plugin’s first-use example turns this request into a plan. It runs locally with Node.js 22 and needs only two files from release 0.2.0. Save the download as 0.2.0.tar.gz in a new folder and open a terminal there. Download Code Maintenance Plugin 0.2.0 from Skills Extract the example and run the helperShell tar -xzf 0.2.0.tar.gz scripts/first_use.mjs examples/first-use-input.json node scripts/first_use.mjs examples/first-use-input.json The output includes the proposed check, go test ./internal/installer, and sets merge_authorized to false. The helper prints a plan. To verify a repair, run the proposed check in the installer repository against the candidate change and record what happened. See the package and installation options in Skills The wider context Related reading The Code Agent’s Playbook · Check a change and evaluate the agent See how an independent check supports a review and how to measure an agent’s reliability across different tasks.
